results.answer: In cosmology, **expansion** means that the distances between widely separated galaxies increase over time because **space itself is stretching**. It is not usually galaxies flying outward from a single point into preexisting space. Rather, the universe has no central expansion point: from any galaxy, sufficiently distant galaxies appear to be receding. A useful analogy is dots drawn on the surface of an inflating balloon. As the surface expands, every dot sees other dots moving away, with more distant dots generally receding faster. This relationship is described by **Hubble’s law**. Cosmic expansion can also be described by a changing **scale factor**, which measures how the universe’s overall size changes. It affects large-scale distances, while objects held together by gravity or other forces—such as galaxies, solar systems, and atoms—do not generally expand along with the universe.

Black holes do not “suck up” everything like cosmic vacuum cleaners. Objects must come close enough for the black hole’s gravity to capture them; from far away, its gravity acts much like that of any other object with the same mass.

results.answer: The Moon has phases because, as it orbits Earth, we see different portions of its sunlit half. The Sun always illuminates half of the Moon. When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its lit side faces mostly away from us, producing a new moon. As it moves around Earth, increasing portions of the illuminated side become visible—waxing to first quarter and full moon—then the visible lit portion decreases, or wanes, through the last quarter back to new moon. The cycle takes about 29.5 days. Lunar phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow; Earth’s shadow causes a lunar eclipse.
